newsitem.title: USA: Clinton starts lobbying for arms deal with Moscow.
newsitem.headline: Clinton starts lobbying for arms deal with Moscow.

text.p: President Bill Clinton moved to counter Republican sniping at a new arms control understanding with Russia on Monday by telephoning members of Congress to explain the Helsinki summit agreement.

Clinton planned to brief lawmakers on his agreement with Russian President Boris Yeltsin last week that none of the six U.S. theatre missile-defence systems now under development will violate the 1972 Anti-Ballistic Missile treaty, a spokesman said.

After Clinton's talks with Yeltsin, the White House hailed the ABM understanding as a major summit success for the Democratic president. But House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich and two other key Republicans issued a statement on Sunday attacking the accord.

Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, House Appropriations Committee Chairman Bob Livingston of Louisiana and Representative Chris Cox of California said the Helsinki agreement would halt development of the most effective ballistic missile defence.
A provision "not to develop, test or deploy space-based interceptors" would place unacceptable contraints on possible technological breakthroughs, they said.

Some Republican lawmakers are pushing a plan to expand a missile monitoring system already used aboard Navy ships into a system using a ballistic shield, a scaled-down version of President Ronald Reagan's "Star Wars" programme that would be banned under the agreement.
"We saw Gingrich's statement. I think that's of special concern to us," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.

Clinton "is especially interested in making sure that members of Congress understand precisely what's agreed to, and that none of the six missile-defence systems that are currently in R&D (research and development) phase would be outside the ABM interpretation and thus prohibited by the ABM treaty," McCurry said.

The White House's quick response to the Republican assault on the ABM issue may have been intended to head off a partisan squabble over the entire package of arms control agreements at Helsinki, including concessions Clinton made to encourage Russia's parliament to approve the START-2 strategic arms reduction treaty.

These included giving cash-starved Russia an extra 12 months to comply with START-2 nuclear warhead limits, which requires the costly dismantling of thousands of warheads -- and an additional four years to destroy the missile silos prohibited under START-2.
The U.S. Senate, which has already ratified the START-2 treaty, would have to approve these changes, perhaps in the form of a rider to a proposed START-3 treaty.

White House aides said Clinton and Yeltsin agreed on the arms control package after the Russian president reluctantly acquiesced to NATO's plan to expand into the old Soviet sphere of influence after a pre-summit torrent of anti-NATO rhetoric.
